rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Qadirin’ may be a circumstantial accusative from the subject of ‘ghadaw’; ‘ala hard’ may depend on it, or itself be the circumstantial phrase with ‘qadirin’ as a second or nested circumstantial.
rows.anchor: " قادرين " حالا من فاعل " غدوا ". و " على حرد " متعلق به،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One lexical view takes hard as anger or fury; a line attributed to al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla uses hard for the rage of fighting lions.
rows.anchor: وأنشد للأشهب ابن رميلة: 4304 أسود شرى لاقت أسود خفية تساقوا على حرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet pairs hard with anger, supporting the sense of fury; the source says the two words are coordinated because their wording differs.
rows.anchor: قيل: ومثله قول الآخر: 4305 إذا جياد الخيل جاءت تردي مملوءة من غضب وحرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hard may mean withholding or scarcity: camels give little milk and a year little rain; Abu Ubayd and al-Qutaybi report this usage.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المنع. من حاردت الإبل: قل لبنها، والسنة: قل مطرها، قاله أبو عبيد والقتبي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word has several vocalized forms and derivatives, including ‘hardan’ and ‘harid’; Arabic also describes a lion as hard and lions as hawarid.
rows.anchor: ويقال: حرد بالكسر يحرد حردا، وقد تفتح فيقال: حردا، فهو حردان وحارد.

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Hard may mean isolation or withdrawal; the verb can mean to withdraw, and a solitary star is called kawkab hard. Al-Asma‘i identifies the usage as Hudhayli.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي: " هي لغة هذيل ". وقيل: الحرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another lexical view is intention or direction: ‘harada yaḥrudu hardaka’ means to intend your direction; a cited verse illustrates the expression.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الحرد القصد. يقال: حرد يحرد حردك، أي: قصد قصدك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse has been interpreted according to all the listed senses of hard.
rows.anchor: وقد فسرت الآية الكريمة بجميع ما ذكرت

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Hard is the proper name of the owners’ particular garden.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الحرد اسم جنتهم بعينها، قاله السدي.

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari says Hard is the name of their village; the author considers both proper-name explanations very remote.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اسم قريتهم، قاله الأزهري. وفيهما بعد بعيد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Qadirin’ most plainly means possessing power, though it may instead derive from estimation and mean restricting the poor.
rows.anchor: قادرين ": إما من القدرة، وهو الظاهر، وإما من التقدير وهو التضييق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Halu‘an is a prospective circumstantial; the following verses explain the quality through a person’s reaction to harm and good.
rows.anchor: هلوعا }: حال مقدرة. والهلع مفسر بما بعده، وهو قوله: " إذا " و " إذا

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Tha‘lab explains the term from the verse itself: a person shows intense distress at harm and hoards good instead of sharing it.
rows.anchor: قال ثعلب: " سألني محمد بن عبد الله ابن طاهر ما الهلع؟ فقلت: قد فسره الله

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd gives the basic lexical sense as the strongest greed and the worst distress.
rows.anchor: وأصله في اللغة على ما قال أبو عبيد أشد الحرص وأسوأ الجزع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation describes rapid panic and agitation when harm touches someone, and quick refusal when good reaches them; the comparison is a swift-moving she-camel.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو الفزع والاضطراب السريع عند مس المكروه، والمنع السريع عند مس الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Jazu‘an’ and ‘manu‘an’ can be overlapping circumstantial states of the pronoun in ‘halu‘an’; the two time phrases modify those states.
rows.anchor: أنهما منصوبان على الحال من الضمير في " هلوعا " وهو العامل فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa’s wording calls ‘jazu‘an’ another circumstantial but can mislead readers into treating it as separate; his stated governor shows the intended overlapping relation.
rows.anchor: جزوعا حال أخرى، والعامل فيها هلوعا ". فقوله: " أخرى " يوهم أنها حال ثانية

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki analyzes both adjectives as predicates of an omitted ‘kana’ or ‘sara’: when harm touches him he becomes distressed, and when good touches him he becomes withholding.
rows.anchor: أو صار مضمرة، أي: إذا مسه الشر كان أو صار جزوعا، وإذا مسه الخير كان أو صار منوعا قاله مكي.

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki also allows the two words to modify ‘halu‘an’, but finds this distant because the time phrase must be understood before its adjective; the author rejects that objection as misplaced.
rows.anchor: الثالث: أنهما نعت ل " هلوعا " قاله مكي. إلا أنه قال: " وفيه بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection to the adjectival analysis is mistaken: its issue is an adverbial phrase preceding its governor, whereas the real prohibited order would put an adjective’s governed element before the adjective.
rows.anchor: فإنه غاية ما فيه تقديم الظرف على عامله، وإنما المحذور تقديم معمول النعت على المنعوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception is from generic ‘the human’; the author compares the construction with the exception in the closing verses of al-‘Asr.
rows.anchor: استثناء من " الإنسان " إذ المراد به الجنس. ومثله: إن الإنسان

rows.speaker: حفص
rows.claim: Hafs reads the later word ‘testimonies’ in the plural to reflect the several kinds; the other readers use the singular because the intended sense is generic.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حفص: " بشهاداتهم " جمعا، اعتبارا بتعدد الأنواع. والباقون بالإفراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Multahadan’ is the object of ‘ajidu’, which here means to find, reach, or resort to; it means a path or destination and, in the poem, an escape or refuge.
rows.anchor: ملتحدا }: مفعول " أجد " لأنها بمعنى: أصيب وألقى. والملتحد هنا: المسلك والمذهب

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited anonymous poet uses ‘multahad’ for a way of escape or recourse from God’s decree.
rows.anchor: يا لهف نفسي ولهفي غير مجدية عني وما من قضاء الله ملتحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghussa is something lodged in the throat and difficult to swallow; the verb is used with a kasra, with ‘ghasin’ and ‘ghasnan’ as forms for the afflicted person.
rows.anchor: الغصة: الشجى، وهو ما ينشب في الحلق فلا ينساغ. ويقال: غصصت بالكسر

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The anonymous poem compares a throat choked by water with a person whose throat is obstructed by something else, witnessing the choking sense of ghussa.
rows.anchor: لو بغير الماء حلقي شرق كنت كالغصان بالماء اعتصاري

rows.speaker: نافع، حمزة، حفص
rows.claim: Nafi‘, Hamza, and Hafs read ‘idh’ as a past-time adverb and ‘adbara’ as the quadriliteral verb; the written consonantal form also permits the alternative reading.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وحمزة وحفص " إذ " ظرفا لما مضى من الزمان، " أدبر " بزنة أكرم

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd prefers ‘idha dabara’ because the next oath phrase also has ‘idha’; he notes that Abd Allah’s reading writes two alifs to represent the form with hamza.
rows.anchor: واختار أبو عبيد قراءة " إذا " قال: لأن بعده " إذا أسفر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also prefers ‘idha’; a report says he objected to ‘adbara’ by saying that only a camel’s back turns away.
rows.anchor: واختار ابن عباس أيضا " إذا " ويحكى أنه لما سمع " أدبر " قال: " إنما يدبر ظهر البعير

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farra’ and al-Zajjaj regard dabara and adbara as synonymous, like other paired verbs meaning that night or day passed or turned away.
rows.anchor: دبر وأدبر، بمعنى أم لا؟ فقيل: هما بمعنى واحد/ يقال: دبر الليل والنهار وأدبر، وقبل وأقبل.

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yunus distinguishes the verbs: dabara means to end, while adbara means to turn away.
rows.anchor: وقال يونس: " دبر انقضى، وأدبر تولى ففرق بينهما

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says dabara means adbara, as qabala means aqbala; one explanation is that night follows day.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: " ودبر بمعنى أدبر كقبل بمعنى أقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites ‘ams al-dabir’ and a poetic line as evidence for dabara meaning past or gone; ‘adbara’ for a rider approaching or leaving is quadriliteral only.
rows.anchor: ومنه قولهم " أمس الدابر " فهذا من دبر، وأمس المدبر

rows.speaker: عيسى بن الفضل وابن السميفع
rows.claim: The common reading has the quadriliteral ‘asfara’; ‘Isa ibn al-Fadl and Ibn al-Sumayfi read the triliteral ‘safara’.
rows.anchor: وقرأ العامة " أسفر " بالألف، وعيسى بن الفضل وابن السميفع " سفر " ثلاثيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Asfara’ means that dawn has cast darkness from its face, expressed as a metaphor.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: طرح الظلمة عن وجهه، على وجه الاستعارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘innaha’ may refer to Hell, the Resurrection, the warning, or be a pronoun of the matter; the Shaykh’s Resurrection interpretation has an unmentioned antecedent and a gender problem.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن قيام الساعة كذا حكاه الشيخ، وفيه شيئان: عوده على غير مذكور

rows.speaker: نصر بن عاصم، ابن محيصن
rows.claim: The common reading has ‘li-ihda’ with hamza; Nasr ibn ‘Asim and Ibn Muhaysin, with a report from Ibn Kathir, read ‘li-hada’ without it, an exceptional form not suitable as a productive analogy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نصر بن عاصم وابن محيصن، وتروى عن ابن كثير " لحدى " بحذف الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exceptional form may be explained by changing hamza to alif and deleting the alif when two vowelless letters meet; regular easing would instead place the hamza between hamza and alif.
rows.anchor: وتوجيهه: أن يكون أبدلها ألفا، ثم حذفت الألف لالتقاء الساكنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘One of the greatest calamities’ means one of the great disasters; the cited verse by Ibn al-Mu‘alla witnesses the phrase, while kubar is the plural of kubra.
rows.anchor: أي: إحدى الدواهي قال: 4395 يا بن المعلى نزلت إحدى الكبر

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Atiyya calls kubar a plural of kabira, but the author suspects that this is an error.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: " جمع كبيرة " وأظنه وهما عليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The sentence may answer the oath beginning ‘by the moon’, or explain ‘kalla’ while the oath is an emphatic parenthesis; the author rejects the second as forced and contrary to the apparent syntax.
rows.anchor: أنها تعليل ل " كلا " والقسم معترض للتوكيد، قاله الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis makes ‘nadhiran’ an accusative specification of ‘ihda’, which conveys greatness; it means warning just as nakir means denunciation, as in the example ‘one of the women in chastity’.
rows.anchor: أنه تمييز عن " إحدى " ، كما ضمنت معنى التعظيم، كأنه قيل: أعظم الكبر إنذارا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra’ treats ‘nadhiran’ as a verbal noun meaning warning, governed by an omitted verb.
rows.anchor: أنه مصدر بمعنى الإنذار أيضا، ولكنه نصب بفعل مقدر، قاله الفراء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj takes ‘nadhir’ as an active form with a passive sense and a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in ‘innaha’.
rows.anchor: أنه فعيل بمعنى مفعل، وهو حال من الضمير في " إنها " قاله الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed governors make it circumstantial from ‘ihda’ understood as magnificent, from the subject of ‘qum’ at the sura’s opening, or a verbal noun governed by ‘anذir’ there.
rows.anchor: أنه حال من الضمير في " إحدى " لتأولها بمعنى العظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further analyses make it circumstantial from ‘al-kubar’ or its pronoun, from ‘li-ihda’ per Ibn ‘Atiyya, or an accusative with an omitted ‘I mean’.
rows.anchor: هو حال من " لإحدى " ، قاله ابن عطية. العاشر: أنه منصوب بإضمار أعني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may instead be governed by an omitted ‘call’ with God intended, or by ‘call’ or ‘convey’ with the Messenger intended; another analysis supplies ‘it became a warning’.
rows.anchor: منصوب بإضمار أعني. الحادي عشر: أنه منصوب ب ادع مقدرا؛ إذ المراد به الله تعالى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Additional circumstantial analyses attach it to the pronoun in ‘kubar’ or ‘huwa’ in the statement that none knows the Lord’s hosts but Him.
rows.anchor: حال من الضمير في " الكبر ". الخامس عشر: أنها حال من " هو

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa treats it as an object of purpose, governed by the verbal meaning in ‘al-kubar’; the author calls that analysis distant.
rows.anchor: قال أبو البقاء: " أو إنها لإحدى الكبر لإنذار البشر

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: When ‘nadhiran’ is circumstantial from a feminine noun, its masculine form is explained by an implied ‘possessing warning’ and a relational sense, according to Abu Ja‘far.
rows.anchor: وإذا جعلت حالا من مؤنث فإنما لم تؤنث لأنها بمعنى ذات إنذار

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة، أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: The common reading has ‘nadhiran’ in the accusative; Ibn Abi ‘Abla and Ubayy ibn Ka‘b read it nominative. If Hell is intended it can be a second predicate or predicate of omitted ‘hiya’; if God or the Messenger is intended, an omitted ‘huwa’ is understood.
rows.anchor: والنصب قراءة العامة، وابن أبي عبلة وأبي بن كعب بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Lil-bashar’ may be an adjective or the object of ‘nadhir’; the preposition li- is extra, strengthening the governor.
rows.anchor: وللبشر " إما صفة. وإمأ مفعول لنذير، واللام مزيدة لتقوية العامل

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh takes ‘hal’ as an ordinary question about the remarkable event of a long age passing over a human who was nothing mentioned; the author calls this interpretation problematic.
rows.anchor: أنها على بابها من الاستفهام المحض، أي: هو ممن يسأل عنه لغرابته

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makki reads ‘hal’ as a confirmatory question addressed to resurrection’s denier: he must admit a long period without people, so the One who created after nonexistence can restore them after death.
rows.anchor: والأحسن أن تكون على بابها للاستفهام الذي معناه التقرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author agrees that the confirmatory question is the correct account; a direct, ordinary question of this kind should not be attributed to God.
rows.anchor: فقد جعلها لاستفهام التقرير لا للاستفهام المحض، وهذا هو الذي يجب أن يكون

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says ‘hal’ can equal ‘qad’ only in a question, yielding ‘has there indeed come’; the question conveys confirmation and ‘qad’ conveys nearness.
rows.anchor: هل بمعنى " قد " في الاستفهام خاصة. والأصل: أهل بدليل قوله

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited line ‘Ahl ra’ana’ is offered as evidence that interrogative ‘hal’ can mean ‘qad’ in an interrogative construction.
rows.anchor: سائل فوارس يربوع بشدتنا أهل رأونا بوادي القف ذي الأكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading, the human had been an unremembered, unmentioned thing; ‘hal’ can stand for ‘qad’ only with a spoken or understood question, though some omit this restriction.
rows.anchor: أن " هل " لا تكون بمعنى " قد " إلا ومعها استفهام/ لفظا كالبيت المتقدم، أو تقديرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reject ‘hal’ as equivalent to ‘qad’ and construe the poetic example as two semantically overlapping particles used together for emphasis despite their different wording.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم لا يجيزه البتة، ويتأول البيت: على أن مما جمع فيه بين حرفي معنى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari’s account also requires a verbal clause, since ‘qad’ applies only to verbs; the author says this restriction causes no difficulty because ‘qad’ cannot directly precede nouns.
rows.anchor: في تقرير كونها على بابها من الاستفهام. " والأحسن أن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Lam yakun’ is more plausibly a circumstantial clause modifying ‘al-insan’; alternatively it is an adjective of ‘hin’ after another adjective, with an implied ‘fihi’.
rows.anchor: التي وقع موقعها " هل ". ومعنى

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A cited poem uses the preposition ba where ‘an’ would normally occur, offered as evidence for combining different particles with overlapping meaning for emphasis.
rows.anchor: فأصبحن لا يسألنني عن بما به

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: Another poem repeats the same preposition in two forms, reinforcing the author’s point that repetition may emphasize a meaning even when the forms differ.
rows.anchor: فلا والله لا يلفى لما بي ولا للما بهم أبدا دواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari did not add the condition that the clause be verbal; the author says this omission is harmless because ‘qad’ does not directly govern nominal clauses.
rows.anchor: لم يذكر الزمخشري غير كونها بمعنى " قد " ، وبقي على الزمخشري قيد آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause ‘lam yakun’ is more clearly a circumstantial from ‘al-insan’; the alternative makes it an adjective of ‘hin’ with an understood pronoun referring to that time.
rows.anchor: والأول أظهر لفظا ومعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition min may mark the starting point, while the reading with ba by Abd Allah ibn Yazid, ‘Ikrima, and Qatada introduces a causal sense; the readings reflect different meanings of ‘mu‘sirat’.
rows.anchor: في " من " أن تكون على بابها من ابتداء الغاية، وأن تكون للسببية.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: One interpretation is clouds nearing the point when winds press them to rain, like crops nearing harvest or a girl nearing puberty; Abu al-Najm’s line witnesses the usage ‘a‘sarat’.
rows.anchor: يقال: أعصرت السحائب، أي: شارفت أن تعصرها الرياح فتمطر

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba cites Abu al-Najm’s verse ‘qad a‘sarat’ as evidence for the usage meaning that the time for a girl’s puberty is near.
rows.anchor: وأنشد ابن قتيبة لأبي النجم: 4466 تمشي الهوينى ساقطا خمارها قد أعصرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without the ‘nearing’ interpretation of ‘a‘sarat’, the form ‘mu‘sirat’ would be expected with a fatḥa on ṣād as a passive participle, since winds press clouds.
rows.anchor: ولولا تأويل " أعصرت " بذلك لكان ينبغي أن تكون المعصرات بفتح الصاد اسم مفعول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: For ‘bil-mu‘sirat’, al-Zamakhshari allows winds ready to press clouds or clouds themselves, since water descends through them, analogous to giving from or by one’s hand.
rows.anchor: أن يراد الرياح التي حان لها أن تعصر السحاب، وأن يراد السحائب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets ‘mu‘sirat’ as winds carrying whirlwinds.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد: المعصرات: الرياح ذوات الأعاصير

rows.speaker: الحسن، قتادة
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Qatada interpret the word as the heavens: water passes from heaven to clouds, as though the heavens are pressing or enabling the pressing.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن وقتادة: هي السماوات. وتأويله: أن الماء ينزل من السماء إلى السحاب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the min-plus-winds interpretation by saying winds form clouds and release their moisture, and reports that God sends winds carrying water from heaven if that report is sound.
rows.anchor: الرياح هي التي تنشىء السحاب وتدر أخلافه، فيصح أن تجعل مبدأ للإنزال

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan proposes ‘mu‘sirat’ as ‘those bringing relief’, but the author questions how a form-IV participle can carry the meaning of the triliteral ‘aṣara’ (to relieve).
rows.anchor: ذكر ابن كيسان: أنه جعل المعصرات بمعنى المغيثات، والعاصر هو المغيث

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari resolves the form issue by taking the hamza as entry into a state: clouds have entered the point at which they are about to bring relief through rain.
rows.anchor: قلت: وجهه أن يراد: اللاتي أعصرن، أي: حان لها أن تعصر، أي: تغيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thajj means pouring in great quantity and force; the verb may be intransitive (‘the water poured’) or transitive (‘I poured it’).
rows.anchor: يقال: ثج الماء بنفسه، أي: انصب وثججته أنا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith phrase pairs ‘ajj’ and ‘thajj’: ‘ajj’ is raising one’s voice in the talbiya and ‘thajj’ is spilling sacrificial blood.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: " أحب العمل إلى الله العج والثج " فالعج: رفع الصوت بالتلبية

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited poem uses ‘thajjajan’ for a copious, forceful flow, witnessing the sense of abundant pouring.
rows.anchor: إذا رجفت فيها رحى مرجحنة تبعج ثجاجا غزير الحوافل

rows.speaker: الأعرج
rows.claim: Al-A‘raj reads ‘thajjahan’ with a final unpointed ḥā’ instead of jīm.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعرج " ثجاحا " بالحاء المهملة أخيرا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls the spillways of water ‘mathajih’ and uses ‘yantajihu’ for water flowing into the valley.
rows.anchor: ومثاجح الماء مصابه، والماء ينثجح في الوادي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says ‘alfafan’ means intertwined and has no singular, like ‘awza‘’ and ‘akhyaf’.
rows.anchor: ألفافا ": ملتفة لا واحد له كالأوزاع والأخياف

rows.speaker: أبو علي الطوسي
rows.claim: Most language authorities analyze ‘alfafan’ as the plural of ‘liff’; Abu ‘Ali al-Tusi’s line ‘jannat liff’ witnesses that form.
rows.anchor: وأنشد أبو علي الطوسي: 4468 جنة لف وعيش مغدق

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa’i analyzes ‘alfafan’ as a plural of ‘lafif’, like sharif/ashraf and shahid/ashhad; a line uses ‘alifaf’ for interwoven groups.
rows.anchor: الثالث: أنه جمع لفيف، قاله الكسائي. ومثله: شريف وأشراف، وشهيد وأشهاد

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba derives the form through pluralization twice: ‘alf’ and ‘lifā’’ first yield ‘liff’, then ‘alfaf’.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن قتيبة. إلا أن الزمخشري، قال: " وما أظنه واجدا له نظيرا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari doubts the double-plural analysis because he knows no parallel such as ‘khudr/akhḍar’ or ‘ḥumr/aḥmar’.
rows.anchor: وما أظنه واجدا له نظيرا من نحو: خضر وأخضار، وحمر وأحمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lack of a productive plural-of-plural pattern does not invalidate Ibn Qutayba’s analysis; ‘liff’ resembles ‘qufl’ and can take the pattern ‘af‘al’, while plural-of-plurals need not be regular.
rows.anchor: لأن جمع الجمع لا ينقاس، ويكفي أن يكون له نظير في المفردات كما رأيت

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari also suggests that ‘alfafan’ could be ‘multaffah’ with its additions removed; the author finds this needlessly strained, since such deletions are chiefly discussed in diminutives and verbal nouns.
rows.anchor: ولو قيل: هو جمع ملتفة بتقدير حذف الزوائد لكان قولا وجيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed answer to ‘idha ja’at’ is the following ‘fa-amma man tagha’, as in the example about Banu Tamim; another supplies an omitted answer meaning ‘the matter is so’.
rows.anchor: في جوابها أوجه، أحدها: قوله: " فأما من طغى " نحو: " إذا جاءك بنو تميم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted oath response, ‘if so, Hell is his abode’; other proposals say ‘they saw’ or ‘they knew’.
rows.anchor: فقدره الزمخشري: فإن الأمر كذلك، أي: فإن الجحيم مأواه

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa says the answer itself governs ‘idha’, whose meaning is expressed by ‘the day when the human remembers’.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: " العامل فيها جوابها، وهو معنى قوله: " يوم يتذكر الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-tamma is a catastrophe that overtops other catastrophes in magnitude; its root also means burying or covering, as in the proverb about a flood covering villages.
rows.anchor: والطامة: الداهية تطم على غيرها من الدواهي لعظمها. والطم: الدفن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘great catastrophe’ here is the second blast of the Trumpet, which brings about that overwhelming event.
rows.anchor: الثانية لأن بها يحصل ذلك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Yawma yatadhakkaru’ may be a substitute for ‘idha’, or an accusative with an omitted verb meaning ‘I mean’; it may also introduce what happens on that day.
rows.anchor: يوم يتذكر }: بدل من " إذا " أو منصوب بإضمار فعل، أي: أعني يوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Fima’ is a fronted predicate, ‘anta’ the delayed subject, and ‘min dhikraha’ attaches to the predicate; the meaning asks what role the Prophet has in reminding them and explaining its time.
rows.anchor: فيم " خبر مقدم، و " أنت " مبتدأ مؤخر و " من ذكراها " متعلق بما تعلق به الخبر

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report from ‘A’isha says the Prophet repeatedly mentioned the Hour and asked about it until this verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري عن عائشة رضي الله عنها: " لم يزل عليه السلام يذكر الساعة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: On ‘A’isha’s report, al-Zamakhshari reads the verse as expressing wonder at the Prophet’s frequent preoccupation with remembering and asking about the Hour.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا هو تعجب من كثرة ذكره لها، كأنه قيل: في أي شغل واهتمام

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: A second analysis pauses after ‘fima’: ‘what is this question?’ Then the Prophet’s sending as the final messenger is itself a sign of the Hour’s nearness, so asking its date is pointless.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الوقف على قوله: " فيم " وهو خبر مبتدأ مضمر، أي: فيم هذا السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author calls that second analysis elegant but rejects it because it departs from the apparent construction and breaks the sentence’s order.
rows.anchor: وهو كلام حسن لولا أنه يخالف الظاهر ومفكك لنظم الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the genitive construct ‘mundhir man’, easing the adjective’s attachment to its object; both construct and nunated forms can refer to present or future warning.
rows.anchor: العامة على إضافة الصفة لمعمولها تخفيفا

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز، أبو جعفر، طلحة، ابن محيصن
rows.claim: ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz, Abu Ja‘far, Talha, and Ibn Muhaysin read ‘mundhirun’ with nunation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمر بن عبد العزيز وأبو جعفر وطلحة وابن محيصن بالتنوين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls nunation the original form and construct an easing; for past warning, he says only the construct works, as in ‘warning Zayd yesterday’.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: " وهو الأصل، والإضافة تخفيف، وكلاهما يصلح للحال والاستقبال

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh instead prefers the construct as the original because verbal governance comes from resemblance and construct is basic in nouns; he objects that the past-tense claim has grammatical qualifications.
rows.anchor: ثم اختار الشيخ أن الأصل الإضافة. قال: " لأن العمل إنما هو بالشبه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author replies that he need not discuss a disputed grammatical detail when he has stated a position shared by the majority.
rows.anchor: قلت: لا يلزمه أن يذكر محل الوفاق، بل هذان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Aw duha-ha’ means the bright part of its evening; it figuratively attaches one time expression to another, naming the two ends of the day, and the cadence favors the construction.
rows.anchor: أي: ضحى العشية، أضاف الظرف إلى ضمير الظرف الآخر تجوزا واتساعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Yawma yafirru’ substitutes for ‘idha’; ‘yughnī’ cannot govern either time expression because it modifies ‘shan’, and a modifier’s governed element cannot precede it.
rows.anchor: بدل من " إذا " ، ولا يجوز أن يكون " يغنيه " عاملا في " إذا " ولا في " يوم " لأنه صفة

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن، الزهري، ابن أبي عبلة، حميد، ابن السميفع
rows.claim: The common reading is ‘yughnihi’ from ‘aghna’; Ibn Muhaysin, al-Zuhri, Ibn Abi ‘Abla, Humayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfi read ‘ya‘nihi’ from ‘‘anani al-amr’, meaning that the matter concerned or affected me.
rows.anchor: والعامة على " يغنيه " من الإغناء، وابن محيصن والزهري وابن أبي عبلة وحميد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘As‘asa’ and ‘sa‘sa‘a’ can mean to approach; in al-‘Ajjaj’s verse the dawn breathes, night clears away, and the night recedes.
rows.anchor: يقال: عسعس وسعسع أقبل. قال العجاج: 4512 حتى إذا الصبح لها تنفسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb may share both opposite senses, or specifically mean to recede in Quraysh usage.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو لهما على طريق الاشتراك. وقيل: أدبر بلغة قريش خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the darkness is arriving; its contrast with ‘when dawn breathes’ supports this sense, which is close to the night’s recession.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أقبل ظلامه، ويرجحه مقابلته بقوله { والصبح إذا تنفس

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines twilight as daylight mingling with night’s darkness at sunset; ishfaq combines care and fear, with ‘min’ emphasizing fear and ‘‘ala’ emphasizing care.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب: " الشفق: اختلاط ضوء النهار بسواد الليل عند غروب الشمس

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari defines twilight as the redness in the west after sunset; its disappearance ends Maghrib and begins ‘Isha’ for most scholars, while Abu Hanifa reportedly once said it was the whiteness and later recanted according to Asad ibn ‘Amr.
rows.anchor: الشفق: الحمرة التي ترى في الغرب بعد سقوط الشمس، وبسقوطه يخرج وقت المغرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There are two twilights, red and white; shafaq and shafaqa are also names for ishfaq, and twilight’s name is linked to delicacy, as is compassion to a tender heart.
rows.anchor: والشفق شفقان: الشفق الأحمر، والآخر الأبيض، والشفق والشفقة اسمان للإشفاق

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poem uses ‘shafaqan’ for fear or tenderness while speaking of loving a life and its death, witnessing the lexical relation to ishfaq.
rows.anchor: تهوى حياتي وأهوى موتها شفقا والموت أكرم نزال على الحرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘wa-ma wasaq’, ‘ma’ may be a relative noun, a relative particle, or an indefinite; wasaq means gathering, as in a wasq measure of sixty ṣa‘s.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن تكون موصولة اسمية أو حرفية، أو نكرة. ووسق، أي: جمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wasaq with kasra is the noun and with fatḥa the verbal noun; food described as mawsuq is gathered, from the verbs wasaqa, ittasaqa, and istawsaqa.
rows.anchor: والوسق بالكسر الاسم، وبالفتح المصدر وطعام موسوق، أي: مجموع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another sense of wasaq is that something acted upon or covered; a poem calls a camel-like force ‘al-wasiq al-mutalabbib’, and a rajaz line describes camels as mustawsiqa.
rows.anchor: وقيل: وسق، أي: عمل فيه. قال الشاعر: 4528 فيوما ترانا صالحين وتارة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra’ says ‘idha ittasaq’ means the moon filled out and became even on full-moon nights; ittisaq is derived from the gathering sense of wasq.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: " وهو امتلاؤه واستواؤه ليالي البدر " وهو افتعل من الوسق

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari identifies ‘inna rabbaka la-bil-mirsad’ as the stated answer to the oath by dawn.
rows.anchor: جواب هذا القسم قيل: مذكور وهو قوله إن ربك لبالمرصاد [الفجر: 14] قاله ابن الأنباري.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the oath’s answer is omitted but understood as a promise to requite each person, indicated by the enumeration of what happened to earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: وقيل: محذوف لدلالة المعنى عليه، أي: لنجازين أحد بما عمل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies ‘He will surely punish’, supported by the account of former peoples being struck down.
rows.anchor: وقدر الزمخشري: " ليعذبن " قال: " يدل عليه ألم تر

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh infers the omitted answer from the preceding sura’s ending: people return to God, who holds them to account.
rows.anchor: وقدره الشيخ بما دلت عليه خاتمة السورة قبله، لإيابهم إلينا وحسابهم علينا

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil treats ‘hal’ as ‘inna’, making the statement that there is indeed an oath for a person of reason; the author rejects this because it cannot be the proposition sworn by the preceding oath.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: " هل هنا في موضع " إن " تقديره: إن في ذلك قسما لذي حجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted noun may be supplied, making the oath by the dawn prayer or by the Lord of dawn.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ثم مضاف محذوف، أي: وصلاة الفجر أو ورب الفجر

rows.speaker: أبو الدينار الأعرابي
rows.claim: Most readers do not nunate ‘al-fajr’, ‘al-watr’, and ‘yasr’; Abu al-Dinar al-A‘rabi nunates all three, treating verse endings like poetic rhymes.
rows.anchor: والعامة على عدم التنوين في " الفجر " و " الوتر " و " يسر ". وأبو الدينار الأعرابي بتنوين الثلاثة

rows.speaker: ابن خالويه
rows.claim: Ibn Khalawayh calls the poetic nunation ‘tanwin al-tarannum’, including nunation at verse endings even for verbs and definite nouns; his quoted couplet illustrates it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن خالويه: " هذا ما روي عن بعض العرب أنه يقف على أواخر القوافي بالتنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians object to the label ‘tanwin al-tarannum’ and prefer ‘tanwin tark al-tarannum’; another type, ‘tanwin al-ghali’, appears on a closed rhyme and is disputed, with different rules from ordinary nunation.
rows.anchor: وقد عاب بعضهم قول النحويين " تنوين الترنم " وقال: بل ينبغي أن يسموه بتنوين ترك الترنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reader has treated the Qur’anic endings like rhyme endings; the author cites similar forms in al-Ahzab and al-Ra‘d as parallels.
rows.anchor: والحاصل أن هذا القارىء أجرى الفواصل مجرى القوافي ففعل فيها ما يفعل فيها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains why the ten nights are indefinite: they are selected nights within the ten, or nights with a distinction absent from others; an article of definite reference would obscure this distinction and disturb the parallel articles in the oath.
rows.anchor: لأنها ليال مخصوصة من بين جنس الليالي العشر بعض منها، أو مخصوصة بفضيلة ليست في غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Idha yasri’ is governed by an omitted verb of swearing: ‘I swear by it at the time it travels by night’.
rows.anchor: منصوب بمحذوف هو فعل القسم، أي: أقسم به وقت سراه

rows.speaker: نافع، أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Nafi‘ and Abu ‘Amr omit the yā’ of ‘yasri’ at pause but retain it in connected recitation.
rows.anchor: وأثبتها وصلا، نافع وأبو عمرو،

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir retains the yā’ in both pausal and connected forms; the other readers omit it in both.
rows.anchor: وأثبتها في الحالين ابن كثير، وحذفها في الحالين الباقون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Retention follows the original imperfect ending; omission follows the written muṣḥaf and verse cadence, like rhyme, while readers who distinguish pause treat it as a resting point.
rows.anchor: وإثباتها هو الأصل لأنها لام فعل مضارع مرفوع، وحذفها لموافقة المصحف

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says night is figuratively described as traveling, though what is meant is that something travels through it.
rows.anchor: ونسب السرى إلى الليل مجاز؛ إذ المراد: يسرى فيه، قاله الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that the night wanes, as in ‘idha adbara’ and ‘idha ‘as‘asa’.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: المراد ينقص كقوله: إذ أدبر [المدثر: 33]، إذا عسعس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hajr means intellect; the author says its explanation has already been given.
rows.anchor: الحجر: العقل. وتقدم الكلام عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first ‘yawma’ is governed by ‘ji’a’ and ‘bi-jahannam’ is its passive deputy; Makki also allows the day expression itself to be the passive deputy.
rows.anchor: منصوب ب " جيء " والقائم مقام الفاعل " بجهنم ". وجوز مكي أن يكون " يومئذ " قائما مقام الفاعل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The second ‘yawma’ may substitute for ‘idha dukkat’; on the Sibawayh approach it shares that phrase’s governor, whereas others understand the governor as repeated.
rows.anchor: فقيل: بدل من " إذا دكت " ، والعامل فيهما " يتذكر " قاله الزمخشري، وهذا هو مذهب سيبويه

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa assigns ‘yaqulu’ as governor of ‘idha dukkat’ and ‘yatadhakkar’ as governor of the second ‘yawma’.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن العامل في " إذا دكت " " يقول " ، والعامل في " يومئذ " " يتذكر " قاله أبو البقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘wa-anna lahu al-dhikra’, ‘anna’ is a fronted predicate, ‘al-dhikra’ its delayed subject, and ‘lahu’ attaches to the predicate.
rows.anchor: أنى " خبر مقدم، و " الذكرى " مبتدأ مؤخر، و " له " متعلق بما تعلق به الظرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Laqad khalaqna’ answers the oath, and kabad means hardship.
rows.anchor: هذا هو المقسم عليه والكبد: المشقة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari derives hardship from a painful, swollen liver and extends it to every kind of toil; mukabada is related, as is kabata (destroy), originally striking someone’s liver.
rows.anchor: وأصله من كبد الرجل كبدا فهو أكبد، إذا وجعت كبده وانتفخت، فاتسع فيه

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labid’s ‘fi kabad’ means being in a hard and difficult situation, witnessing the hardship sense.
rows.anchor: قال لبيد: 4573 يا عين هلا بكيت أربد إذ قمنا وقام الخصوم في كبد

rows.speaker: ذو الإصبع
rows.claim: Dhu al-Isba‘’s line uses ‘fi kabad’ for severe trouble and difficulty, likewise witnessing the word’s meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال ذو الإصبع: 4574 لي ابن عم لوان الناس في كبد لظل محتجرا بالنبل يرميني

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو، ابن كثير، الكسائي
rows.claim: Abu ‘Amr, Ibn Kathir, and al-Kisa’i read ‘fakka’ and ‘at‘ama’ as past-tense verbs with ‘raqabatan’ accusative; these verbs explain ‘iqtahama’.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وابن كثير والكسائي " فك " فعلا ماضيا، " ورقبة " نصبا " أو أطعم " فعلا ماضيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining readers take ‘fakku’ as a nominative noun with ‘raqabatin’ genitive and ‘it‘amun’ nominative; an implied topic means ‘it is freeing a slave or feeding’, with a permissive sense.
rows.anchor: والباقون " فك " برفع الكاف اسما، " رقبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted noun, ‘iqtiham’, is required after ‘wa-ma adraka ma al-‘aqaba’ so the verbal noun ‘fakku’ explains a verbal noun rather than the concrete obstacle itself.
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام حذف مضاف دل عليه " فلا اقتحم " تقديره: وما أدراك ما اقتحام العقبة

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين، أبو رجاء
rows.claim: ‘Ali and Abu Raja’ read ‘fakka aw at‘ama’ as verbs but put ‘dha’ in the accusative; al-Hasan also has the accusative ‘dha’ with ‘it‘am’.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أمير المؤمنين وأبو رجاء " فك أو أطعم " فعلين كما تقدم، إلا أنهما نصبا " ذا " بالألف

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads ‘it‘am’ as a noun and ‘dha’ in the accusative; on these readings ‘dha’ is the object of feeding, with ‘yatiman’ appositional or adjectival.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن " إطعام " و " ذا " بالألف أيضا وهو على هاتين القراءتين مفعول " أطعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common ‘dhi’ is an adjective of the day by metaphor: calling a day hungry intensifies the description, like calling a night standing or a day fasting; the agent of feeding is omitted.
rows.anchor: وهو في قراءة العامة " ذي " بالياء نعتا ل " يوم " على سبيل المجاز، وصف اليوم بالجوع مبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Omitting only the agent is one of the constructions Basran grammarians permit regularly; the author says he has treated the rule fully elsewhere.
rows.anchor: والفاعل لإطعام محذوف، وهذا أحد المواضع التي يطرد فيها حذف الفاعل وحده عند البصريين

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines masghaba as hunger with fatigue, sometimes thirst with fatigue; the related words come from roots for hunger, dust-poverty, and kinship.
rows.anchor: والمسغبة: الجوع مع التعب، وربما قيل في العطش مع التعب، قال الراغب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari neatly groups masghaba, maqraba, and matraba as derived forms from hunger, closeness in kinship, and becoming poor.
rows.anchor: قال: " والمسغبة والمقربة والمتربة مفعلات من سغب إذا جاع وقرب في النسب وترب إذا افتقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Tariba’ means becoming so poor that the skin touches dust; ‘atraba’ with hamza instead means becoming wealthy, as in athra.
rows.anchor: يقال ترب، أي: افتقر حتى لصق جلده بالتراب. فأما أترب بالألف فبمعنى استغنى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes ‘thumma’ as a delay in rank and virtue, not time: faith precedes all deeds and is their necessary basis.
rows.anchor: لتراخي الإيمان وتباعده في الرتبة والفضيلة عن العتق والصدقة، لا في الوقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation means that a person ultimately meets death in faith, a condition for benefiting from acts of devotion.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى على: ثم كان في عاقبة أمره من الذين وافوا الموت على الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation makes ‘thumma’ signal delay in the presentation of the ideas.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التراخي في الذكر وتقدم تفسيره

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad is quoted as deriving duha and dawha from dhaw (‘light’), with alif and wāw replacing the letter ḥā’; the author calls this nearly fabricated despite the scholar’s standing.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: " إن الضحى والضحوة مشتقان من الضح وهو النور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For ‘jallaha’, the subject may be the pronoun of daylight or may refer to God; its object pronoun may refer to the sun, darkness, the world, or the earth.
rows.anchor: الفاعل ضمير النهار، وقيل: عائد على الله تعالى. والضمير المنصوب: إما للشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘idha’ clauses raise a syntactic problem: a conditional needs an answer, while a purely temporal phrase needs a governor; the oath verb is present-time and cannot straightforwardly govern a future time phrase.
rows.anchor: لأنه إن جعل شرطا اقتضى جوابا، ولا جواب لفظا، وتقديره غير صالح

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari answers that an oath wāw suppresses its verb and stands for both the verb and preposition; following coordinating wāws can therefore govern the same accusative and genitive pattern.
rows.anchor: واو القسم مطرح معها إبراز الفعل أطراحا كليا، فكان لها شأن خلاف شأن الباء

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh rejects the claim that a conjunction governs by standing in for a governor; he says the governor of the coordinated element is the same as for its antecedent, though he does not insist on that point against al-Zamakhshari.
rows.anchor: فليس هذا بالمختار، أعني أن يكون حرف العطف عاملا لقيامه مقام العامل

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh says the verse coordinates two nouns with matching case roles, rather than coordinating across two governors, and offers ‘passing by Zayd standing and ‘Amr sitting’ as the pattern.
rows.anchor: وإنما هو من باب عطف اسمين: مجرور ومنصوب على اسمين: مجرور ومنصوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Shaykh cites a line in Sibawayh that coordinates a genitive and a nominative with another genitive and nominative as a parallel construction.
rows.anchor: جالسا " وأنشد سيبويه في كتابه:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Shaykh invokes the Sibawayh poem as a case of coordinating a genitive plus nominative pair with another pair; the author says this concedes the disputed coordination, though the poem has an additional complication.
rows.anchor: فهذا من عطف مجرور ومرفوع، على مجرور ومرفوع، والعطف على عاملين فيه أربعة مذاهب

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil says the last two wāws in the oath sequence coordinate nouns, while the first is like the prepositional wāw and the tā’ of swearing.
rows.anchor: الواوان الأخيرتان ليستا بمنزلة الأولى، ولكنهما الواوان اللتان تضمان الأسماء إلى الأسماء

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan permits an explicit oath verb with the wāw, as in ‘I swear by God that Zayd is standing’; the author says this objection does not bind al-Zamakhshari’s position.
rows.anchor: أجاز ابن كيسان التصريح بفعل القسم مع الواو، فتقول: أقسم - أو أحلف - والله

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh identifies the deeper puzzle as finding a governor for a future ‘idha’ after an oath: the present oath verb, an implied event, the oath object itself, and an implied circumstantial all face objections.
rows.anchor: والذي نقوله: إن المعضل هو تقدير العامل في " إذا " بعد الأقسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Shaykh’s preference that conjunction does not itself govern does not compel al-Zamakhshari, who chooses the alternative grammatical doctrine.
rows.anchor: فقوله: " إن المختار أن حرف العطف لا يعمل لقيامه مقام العامل فلا يلزم أبا القاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author insists that the construction does involve two governors: oath wāw governs the genitive and the oath verb governs the time adverb, with both sets of complements coordinated.
rows.anchor: أن قوله: { والنهار إذا جلاها } هنا معمولان أحدهما مجرور وهو " النهار " والآخر منصوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Sibawayh poem cited by the Shaykh acknowledges coordination across the two governors, even though the Shaykh relies on Sibawayh’s authority.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله: " وأنشد سيبويه إلى آخره " فهو اعتراف منه بأنه من العطف على عاملين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning Ibn Kaysan’s permission to state an oath verb does not refute al-Zamakhshari, because the latter need not share Ibn Kaysan’s view.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله " أجاز ابن كيسان / فلا يلزمه مذهبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Shaykh’s example with a second time phrase preceding the coordinated noun does parallel the verse’s governors, though it raises a separate issue of repeating the construction.
rows.anchor: فصحيح لما فيه من تقديم الظرف الثاني على المجرور المعطوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Khalil’s description as ‘disfavored’ supports prohibition rather than rebutting al-Zamakhshari; the Shaykh has either softened the term or misunderstood it.
rows.anchor: غاية ما في الباب أنه عبر بالاستكراه عن المنع، أو لم يفهم المنع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted construct such as ‘rising of the star’ can be the governor; the author says an oath now may refer to an object that will exist later, so the tense mismatch is no objection.
rows.anchor: بل يجوز تقديره: وهو العامل، ولا يلزم ما قال من اختلاف الزمانين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A deleted governor before ‘idha’ is possible as a prospective circumstantial; the oath verb still governs it, and the circumstantial may be understood prospectively.
rows.anchor: ولا جائز أن يقدر محذوف قبل الظرف،فيكون قد عمل فيه " إلى آخره ليس بممنوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the sworn object is a physical entity, one can supply an event, making the temporal phrase a circumstantial attached to that event; Ibn al-Hajib addressed the question and the author notes extended debate.
rows.anchor: هذه المسألة سئل عنها الشيخ أبو عمرو ابن الحاجب ونقح فيها السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘yaghshaha’, the object pronoun may refer to the sun or the earth.
rows.anchor: يغشاها } المفعول للشمس. وقيل: للأرض،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present ‘yaghshaha’ replaces the past form used around it to maintain the verse endings; ‘idha ghashiyaha’ would break the sound pattern.
rows.anchor: وجيء ب " يغشاها " مضارعا دون ما قبله وما بعده مراعاة للفواصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Inna sa‘y akum la-shatta’ is the oath’s answer, though the answer could instead be omitted as in comparable passages.
rows.anchor: هذا جواب القسم. ويجوز أن يكون محذوفا، كما قيل في نظائره المتقدمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objects of ‘a‘ta’, ‘ittaqa’, and ‘saddaqa’ are omitted, including the complement introduced by ‘‘ala’, because the deeds themselves are the focus; the objects of withholding and self-sufficiency are omitted similarly.
rows.anchor: حذف مفعولي " أعطى " ومفعول " اتقى " ومفعول " صدق " المجرور ب " على "؛ لأن الغرض ذكر هذه الأحداث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We will ease him toward hardship’ may be a rhetorical counterpart to easing toward ease, or ‘nuyassir’ may mean prepare, which can apply to either ease or hardship.
rows.anchor: إما من باب المقابلة لقوله: { فسنيسره لليسرى } ، وإما لأن نيسره بمعنى نهيئه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Ma’ may be a simple negation (‘his wealth will not benefit him’) or a rhetorical, denying question.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن تكون " ما " نفيا، وأن تكون استفهاما إنكاريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Taradda’ may mean perishing, or being wrapped in a shroud, a euphemism for death; two poems use the shroud sense.
rows.anchor: تردى } إما من الهلاك، أو من تردى بأكفانه، وهو كناية عن الموت

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي بن الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: The common reading is ‘yatazakka’, the imperfect of tazakka; al-Hasan ibn ‘Ali reads ‘yazakka’, assimilating the tā’ into zāy.
rows.anchor: والحسن بن علي بن الحسن بن علي أمير المؤمنين يزكى بإدغام التاء في الزاي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The clause may be a circumstantial from the subject of ‘yu’ti’, meaning he gives while purifying himself through the gift.
rows.anchor: أنها في موضع الحال من فاعل " يؤتي " أي: يؤتيه متزكيا به

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari also allows the clause to have no syntactic position and to replace the relative clause of ‘alladhi’; the Shaykh finds this strained.
rows.anchor: على أنها بدل من صلة " الذي " ذكرهما الزمخشري. وجعل الشيخ متكلفا

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib says saja means to become still, as with settling sea waves, or slack as with an unfocused eye; the dead are figuratively ‘covered’ by a shroud.
rows.anchor: قيل: معناه سكن، ومنه: سجا البحر يسجو سجوا، أي: سكنت أمواجه

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-A‘sha’s poem contrasts a heaving sea with a still one, witnessing saja as calm or stillness.
rows.anchor: وقال الأعشى: 4589 وما ذنبنا إن جاش بحر ابن عمكم وبحرك ساج

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra’ says saja means ‘grew dark’; Ibn al-A‘rabi intensifies this to ‘became very dark’, with a poem describing the moonlit, dark night.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: " أظلم ". وقال ابن الأعرابي: " اشتد ظلامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views take saja as receding, or as its opposite; the author notes the ambiguity without choosing between them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: سجا، أي: أدبر وقيل بعكسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root is one of the verbs with wāw; its final vowel is inclined for the rhyme, as with duha, which also comes from a wāw verb.
rows.anchor: وهو من ذوات الواو، وإنما أميل لموافقة رؤوس الآي، كالضحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Ma wadda‘aka’ is the oath’s answer; the common reading doubles dāl from tawdi‘, while ‘Urwa, his son Hisham, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi ‘Abla read a light dāl from wada‘ (‘leave’).
rows.anchor: والعامة على تشديد الدال من التوديع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although standard Arabic generally uses taraka in place of wada‘ and its derivatives, the verb occurs in poetry; two anonymous poems demonstrate it.
rows.anchor: والمشهور في اللغة الاستغناء عن ودع ووذر واسم فاعلهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says tawdi‘ intensifies wada‘, since someone who bids farewell while leaving has emphatically abandoned the person.
rows.anchor: قيل: والتوديع مبالغة في الودع؛ لأن من ودعك مفارقا فقد بالغ في تركك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Ma qala’ means ‘he did not hate you’; the usual imperfect qalahu has kasra, while Tayyi’ uses fatḥa, and a poem witnesses the latter.
rows.anchor: قلاه يقليه بكسر العين في المضارع، وطيىء تقول: قلاه يقلاه بالفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of ‘qala’ is omitted because it is understood, and for the verse cadence; the same ellipsis follows ‘fa-awa’ and what comes after it.
rows.anchor: وحذف مفعول " قلى " مراعاة للفواصل مع العلم به وكذا بعد " فآوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has sukūn in all four occurrences of ‘‘usr’ and ‘yusr’; Ibn Waththab, Abu Ja‘far, and ‘Isa read them with ḍamma, whose status as original or lengthened form is disputed.
rows.anchor: العامة على سكون السين في الكلم الأربع، وابن وثاب وأبو جعفر وعيسى بضمها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbas explains the repeated definite ‘hardship’ and indefinite ‘ease’ with the saying that one hardship will not overcome two eases; a report also attributes the saying to the Prophet, who came out laughing.
rows.anchor: ولذلك روي عن ابن عباس: " لن يغلب عسر يسرين " وروي أيضا مرفوعا أنه عليه السلام خرج يضحك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic normally uses the definite article on a repeated noun when it refers to the same man or messenger, but an indefinite repeated noun refers to a different one; the author applies this to the verse’s one hardship and two eases.
rows.anchor: أن العرب إذا أتت باسم ثم أعادته مع الألف واللام كان هو الأول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls Ibn ‘Abbas’s interpretation a hopeful reading that takes God’s promise in the fullest sense; alternatively, the second sentence either repeats the first for emphasis or independently promises another ease after hardship.
rows.anchor: هذه عمل على الظاهر وبناء على قوة الرجاء، وأن موعد الله لا يحمل إلا على أوفى ما يحتمله اللفظ

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the hardship remains one whether its definite article is referential or generic; indefinite ‘ease’ covers part of its class, and an independent second promise can name another ease.
rows.anchor: وإنما كان العسر واحدا لأنه لا يخلو: إما أن يكون تعريفه للعهد

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa likewise says the two definite hardships are identical and the two indefinite eases are separate, deriving the saying about one hardship and two eases.
rows.anchor: العسر في الموضعين واحد؛ لأن الألف واللام توجب تكرير الأول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Since ‘ma‘a’ normally means accompaniment, al-Zamakhshari says the ease follows hardship quickly enough to be figuratively concurrent, consoling and strengthening hearts.
rows.anchor: أراد أن الله تعالى يصيبهم بيسر بعد العسر الذي كانوا فيه بزمان قريب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the indefinite ‘yusran’ as magnifying the ease; Ibn Mas‘ud’s codex has it only once.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت ما معنى هذا التنكير؟ قلت: التفخيم كأنه قيل: إن مع العسر يسرا عظيما

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Explaining the Prophet’s report despite Ibn Mas‘ud’s single ‘yusran’, al-Zamakhshari takes the magnified ease to include the ease of both abodes, thus amounting to two.
rows.anchor: قلت: " كأنه قصد باليسرين ما في قوله " يسرا " من معنى التفخيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Laqad khalaqna’ is the answer to the oath; ‘fi ahsani taqwim’ means ‘in a configuration of the best form’, with an omitted noun understood.
rows.anchor: هذا هو المقسم عليه. قوله: { في أحسن تقويم } صفة لمحذوف

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa takes ‘fi ahsani taqwim’ as a circumstantial of ‘al-insan’, understanding taqwim as constitution rather than the act of shaping, which properly belongs to the Creator.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: في أحسن تقويم في موضع الحال من " الإنسان

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa also allows an omitted construct (‘best uprightness of form’) or an extra ‘fi’, yielding ‘we formed him in the best form’; the author says these complications are unnecessary.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون " في " زائدة، اي: " قومناه أحسن تقويم " انتهى، ولا حاجة إلى هذه التكلفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Asfala safilin’ may be a circumstantial modifying the object, or an adjective of an omitted place (‘a place lower than the lowest’).
rows.anchor: يجوز فيه وجهان، أحدهما: أنه حال من المفعول. والثاني: أنه صفة لمكان محذوف

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ‘Abd Allah reads ‘al-safilin’ with the definite article.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله " السافلين " معرفا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The exception may be connected: people were lowered beneath the lowest in creation and form, referring to the people of Hell.
rows.anchor: أنه متصل على أن المعنى: رددناه أسفل من سفل خلقا وتركيبا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Alternatively, the exception is disconnected: after giving the human the best form, God lowers him through age and physical decline, while righteous elderly believers receive lasting reward.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أنه منقطع على أن المعنى: ثم رددناه بعد ذلك التقويم والتحسين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Qadhan’ may be a verbal noun reinforcing the sparks made by striking, or a circumstantial describing horses striking stones with their hooves to make fire.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون مصدرا مؤكدا؛ لأن الإيراء من القدح

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says ‘qadhan’ is governed as ‘dabḥan’; he allows an omitted verb, the preceding active participle, or a circumstantial as its governor.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: " انتصب بما انتصب به ضبحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire produced by hooves is called ‘nar al-habahib’; a poem uses that name for the sparks from struck blades.
rows.anchor: وتسمى تلك النار التي تخرج من الحوافر نار الحباحب. قال: 4619 تقد السلوقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Subhan’ is a time adverb meaning at dawn; aghara means to raid by surprise for plunder, killing, or capture, and a poem witnesses the raid sense.
rows.anchor: صبحا: ظرف، أي: التي تغير وقت الصبح يقال: أغار يغير إغارة باغت عدوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghara or aghara can also mean descending into a low valley; this is a rare dialectal usage.
rows.anchor: و " غار " لغية، وأغار وغار أيضا: نزل الغور وهو المنهبط من الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes all the racing, sparking, and raiding descriptions as horses; their descriptions are coordinated in sequence as in a cited poetic example.
rows.anchor: فقيل: الخيل، أي والخيل العاديات، فالموريات، فالمغيرات

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
rows.claim: A view attributed to the Commander of the Faithful takes the descriptions as camels running from ‘Arafa to Muzdalifa and Mina; a poem by Safiyya bint ‘Abd al-Muttalib supports this interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التقدير: والإبل العاديات من عرفة إلى مزدلفة، ومن مزدلفة إلى منى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret ‘al-muriyat’ as a group scheming in war; the idiom ‘I will light you up’ means ‘I will plot against you’.
rows.anchor: وقيل: " فالموريات " أي: الجماعة التي تمكر في الحرب. تقول العرب: لأورين لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Fa-atharna’ coordinates a verb with a noun phrase because the noun is a relative participle standing for a verb; the underlying sequence is ‘those that ran, sparked, raided, then raised’.
rows.anchor: عطف الفعل على الاسم؛ لأن الاسم في تأويل الفعل لوقوعه صلة ل أل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari describes the verb as coordinated with the verb for which the active participle stands.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: " معطوف على الفعل الذي وضع اسم الفاعل موضعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘bihi’ may refer to dawn, meaning that they raised dust at dawn; the author calls this good because dawn is explicitly named.
rows.anchor: أنها ضمير الصبح، أي: فأثرن في وقت الصبح غبارا. وهذا حسن؛ لأنه مذكور بالصريح

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The pronoun may instead refer to the unmentioned place, since stirring dust requires a place and the scene and verb imply one; al-Zamakhshari calls it the place of the raid.
rows.anchor: أنه عائد على المكان، وإن لم يجر له ذكر؛ لأن الإثارة لا بد لها من مكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view makes the pronoun refer to the enemy, implied by the charging horses.
rows.anchor: أنه ضمير العدو الذي دل عليه " والعاديات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has a light thā’ from athara (‘scatter and raise’); Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi ‘Abla read it doubled.
rows.anchor: وقرأ العامة بتخفيف الثاء، من أثار كذا: إذا نشره وفرقه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the doubled reading either as making dust manifest, or through a far-fetched metathesis from thawrna and conversion of wāw to hamza; the author says the latter is very remote and not a regular sound change.
rows.anchor: وخرجه الزمخشري على وجهين: الأول بمعنى فأظهرن به غبارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Changing an open wāw to hamza is not a regular rule; the few examples such as ahad and anah are exceptional, so they do not justify this derivation.
rows.anchor: الواو همزة، فصار " أثرن " وهذا بعيد جدا. وعلى تقدير التسليم فقلب الواو المفتوحة همزة لا ينقاس إنما جاءت منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naq‘ means dust; poems by an unnamed poet and Ibn Rawaha use it for dust raised by horses.
rows.anchor: والنقع: الغبار وأنشد: 4623 يخرجن من مستطار النقع دامية

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd says naq‘ can mean raising one’s voice and supports it with a line about a sincere cry.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيد: " النقع رفع الصوت " وأنشد: 4625 فمتى ينقع صراخ صادق

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari also permits naq‘ to mean a cry, citing a Prophetic expression and a line by Labid; on this reading the horses stirred the people attacked at dawn.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: " ويجوز أن يراد بالنقع الصياح، من قوله عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the cry interpretation of naq‘, the preposition ba means ‘in’, and the pronoun refers back to the place where the raid occurred.
rows.anchor: لمكان الذي فيه الإغارة كما تقدم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Hatta’ marks the endpoint of ‘alhakum’ and is coordinated with that verb.
rows.anchor: حتى ": غاية لقوله " ألهاكم " وهو عطف عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has ṣād still; Salam ibn Sulaymān reads ‘al-‘aṣri’ and ‘al-ṣabri’ with kasra. Ibn ‘Atiyya allows this only at pause through vowel transfer, while an Abu ‘Amr report uses an imala-like kasra on the bā’.
rows.anchor: وسلام " والعصر " والصبر " بكسر الصاد والباء. قال ابن عطية: ولا يجوز إلا في الوقف

rows.speaker: الهذلي
rows.claim: Al-Hudhali reports the kasra reading of ‘al-‘aṣr’, ‘al-ṣabr’, ‘al-fajr’, and ‘al-watr’ from Harun and Ibn Musa on Abu ‘Amr in both pause and connected recitation.
rows.anchor: قال الهذلي: " والعصر والصبر، والفجر، والوتر، بكسر ما قبل الساكن في هذه كلها

rows.speaker: ابن خالويه
rows.claim: Ibn Khalawayh also describes Abu ‘Amr’s ‘al-ṣabri’ as vowel transfer without limiting the report to pause.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن خالويه: " والصبر " بنقل الحركة عن أبي عمرو " فأطلق ايضا

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل
rows.claim: Abu al-Fadl describes transferring the final rā’s vowel to bā’ before a pause as widespread Arabic, marking inflection, avoiding two adjacent vowelless letters, and preserving pause-sukūn.
rows.anchor: بنقل حركة الراء إلى الباء يحتاج إلى أن يأتي ببعض الحركة في الوقف

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The anonymous poetic examples ‘wa-ṣṭifāqan bi-r-rajul’ and ‘ana Jarir … wa-Sa‘d fi al-qaṣr’ witness transferring a vowel before a consonant cluster.
rows.anchor: بالرجل يريد بالرجل. وقال آخر: 4637 أنا جرير كنيتي أبو عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Vowel transfer also occurs with ḍamma, as in the cited ‘idh jadda al-naqru’.
rows.anchor: والنقل جائز في الضمة أيضا كقوله: 4638............. إذ جد النقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Al-‘aṣr’ can mean both night and day; a poem calls them the two ‘aṣrs’ and glosses them as a day and a night.
rows.anchor: والعصر: الليلة واليوم قال: 4639 ولن يلبث العصران يوم وليلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Al-insan’ is generic, with the exception that follows serving as evidence for this broad scope.
rows.anchor: المراد به العموم بدليل الاستثناء منه، وهو من جملة أدلة العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has a still sīn in ‘khusr’; Zayd ibn ‘Ali, Ibn Hurmuz, and one transmission from ‘Asim use ḍamma, like ‘‘usr’ and ‘yusr’.
rows.anchor: وقرأ العامة " لفي خسر " بسكون السين. وزيد بن علي وابن هرمز وعاصم في رواية بضمها

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub derives ‘ma‘un’ as fa‘ul from ma‘n, ‘a small thing’, citing ‘ma-lahu ma‘na’ for someone with little property.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أنه فاعول من المعن وهو الشيء القليل. يقال: " ماله معنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second derivation makes it a passive participle of ‘a‘ana’; its original form would be ma‘wun, with metathesis and vowel change producing the attested form and pattern maf‘ul.
rows.anchor: أنه اسم مفعول من أعانه يعينه. والأصل: معوون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That derivation has three irregularities: a passive from form IV normally has the maf‘al pattern, it uses metathesis, and it changes an unvocalized weak letter to alif; the author calls comparison with ‘taba’ and ‘ṣama’ weak.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا الوجه شذوذ من ثلاثة أوجه، أولها: كون مفعول جاء من أفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible answer to the final irregularity is that the wāw was vocalized before metathesis, as the reconstructed ‘ma‘wun’ suggests.
rows.anchor: وقد يجاب عن الثالث: بأن الواو متحركة في الأصل قبل القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred derivation is ma‘una, with alif replacing the feminine tā’; on this account ma‘un means anything people use and benefit from, such as an axe, bucket, or fire striker.
rows.anchor: وأحسنها: أنه كل ما يستعان به وينتفع به كالفأس والدلو والمقدحة

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-A‘sha’s poem uses ‘ma‘unihi’ for useful provisions or resources; it is offered as poetic evidence for the preferred sense.
rows.anchor: وأنشد قول الأعشى: 4657 بأجود منه بماعونه إذا ما سماؤهم لم تغم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of ‘yamna‘un’ is omitted because people or petitioners are understood, or because the point is to condemn withholding trifling things that everyone recognizes should not be denied.
rows.anchor: ولم يذكر المفعول الأول للمنع: إما للعلم به، أي: يمنعون الناس أو الطالبين
